articles.title: Professor é espancado no Centro do Rio após defender mulher | G1
articles.standfirst: André Aires foi atacado por um grupo de homens na manhã de domingo (15), depois de gritar por ajuda ao presenciar uma mulher sendo agredida. Ele sofreu traumatismo craniano, passou por cirurgia e está internado no Hospital Miguel Couto.
articles.summary: Professor espancado no Centro do Rio, André Aires sofreu traumatismo craniano ao tentar defender uma mulher e está em estado grave no Hospital Miguel Couto.
articles.body:
Professor é espancado após tentar defender mulher de agressão no Centro do Rio — Foto: Redes sociais

O professor, escritor e ator André Luís de Oliveira, conhecido como André Aires, está internado em estado grave no Hospital Municipal Miguel Couto, na Zona Sul do Rio, após ser espancado por um grupo de homens na manhã de domingo (15), no Centro do Rio. Um dos agressores foi preso em flagrante.

Segundo o relato do companheiro de André, o ataque aconteceu depois que o professor tentou impedir uma agressão contra uma mulher nas proximidades da Cruz Vermelha. O companheiro relata que o agressor da mulher foi quem incitou o espancamento do professor.

O homem foi preso em flagrante, responde por tentativa de homicídio e foi identificado como Victor Hugo de Araújo Palmeira.

André sofreu traumatismo craniano e múltiplos ferimentos pelo corpo e precisou passar por uma cirurgia. O caso é investigado pela 5ª DP (Mem de Sá).

O casal passeava com os dois cachorros, por volta das 8h, quando viu um homem puxando uma mulher pela roupa e dando tapas nela. A agressão acontecia perto do cruzamento das ruas Carlos Sampaio e Carlos de Carvalho.

Ao perceber a situação, André começou a gritar por ajuda e pediu que o homem parasse de bater na mulher. Uma viatura da Polícia Militar que estava nas proximidades foi até o local. De acordo com o namorado, os policiais desceram do veículo, mas a mulher já havia conseguido se afastar. A equipe deixou a região sem prender o agressor.

Quando o casal começou a voltar para casa, a mulher que acompanhava o homem passou a perseguir André, segundo o relato. Ela teria feito ofensas homofóbicas e ameaçado o professor.

Pouco depois, o homem que havia agredido a mulher e outros integrantes do grupo partiram para cima de André, nas proximidades do Bar do Bigode, na Rua Carlos Sampaio.

Agressões continuaram dentro de estabelecimentos

Segundo o namorado, André tentou se proteger dentro do bar, mas foi perseguido pelos agressores. O professor teria sido atingido com cadeiras, mesas e garrafas, além de ter a cabeça batida contra uma geladeira.

Na tentativa de escapar, ele entrou na área da cozinha do estabelecimento. Ainda de acordo com o relato, funcionários o retiraram do espaço e o colocaram novamente no salão. Em seguida, André foi levado à força para a rua, onde as agressões continuaram.

O namorado contou que também pediu ajuda em outro estabelecimento, próximo a uma farmácia, mas não conseguiu interromper o espancamento. Ele estava com os dois cachorros do casal e disse que teve medo de também ser atacado.

Victor Hugo de Araujo Palmeira, preso por tentativa de homicídio — Foto: Reprodução

André acabou caindo desacordado na calçada, com ferimentos e sangramento. O namorado contou que, naquele momento, chegou a acreditar que ele estivesse morto.

André foi socorrido pelo Corpo de Bombeiros enquanto o agressor foi preso em flagrante tentando fugir do local. Nesta segunda-feira, a prisão dele foi convertida em flagrante.

Victor Hugo responde por tentativa de homicídio.

Amigos e familiares buscam acesso às imagens das câmeras de segurança da região para ajudar a identificar todos os envolvidos e esclarecer a dinâmica do ataque.

articles.title: Morre menino de 11 anos após acidente na BR-153 em Onda Verde | G1
articles.standfirst: Acidente ocorreu no sábado (14), em Onda Verde (SP). Miguel Nobre Muniz ficou internado na Unidade de Tratamento Intensivo (UTI) do Hospital da Criança e Maternidade de Rio Preto (SP).
articles.summary: Miguel Nobre Muniz estava internado no Hospital da Criança e Maternidade de Rio Preto após o carro em que estava com a mãe ser atingido por um caminhão na BR-153.
articles.body:
O menino de 11 anos que estava internado em estado grave após o acidente de carro que matou a mãe dele morreu nesta segunda-feira (16), em São José do Rio Preto (SP). A informação foi confirmada pelo pai, Márcio Muniz, nas redes sociais, e pelo hospital ao g1 .

O acidente aconteceu na manhã de sábado (14), no quilômetro 41 da Rodovia Transbrasiliana (BR-153), em Onda Verde (SP). No vídeo publicado, Márcio agradece a mobilização de igrejas, amigos e até desconhecidos em oração pela melhora do filho, Miguel Nobre Muniz.

Morre menino de 11 anos que ficou em estado grave após acidente de carro que matou a mãe na BR-153 em Onda Verde (SP) — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

"Pessoas que nem me conheciam, até de outro pais. Muito obrigado, mas o Miguel acabou de falecer. Eu perdi o meu garoto", diz o pai no vídeo.

Miguel ficou internado na Unidade de Tratamento Intensivo (UTI) por três dias e não resistiu aos ferimentos. Até a última atualização desta reportagem, não há informações sobre velório.

Juliana Nobre morre após carro ser arrastado por caminhão em rodovia em Onda Verde (SP) — Foto: Reprodução/Instagram e Polícia Rodoviária Federal/Divulgação

Segundo o boletim de ocorrência, a mãe de Miguel, Juliana de Souza Nobre, de 37 anos, tentava cruzar o trevo para acessar a pista sentido Rio Preto, quando o carro foi atingido por um caminhão , que trafegava no sentido Nova Granada (SP). O veículo foi arrastado por 40 metros.

A mulher morreu no local. Miguel, que também estava no carro, chegou a ser reanimado pelos bombeiros no local. Depois, foi socorrido e encaminhado em estado grave ao Hospital da Criança e Maternidade (HCM), em Rio Preto.

articles.title: Comerciante baleado na cabeça durante assalto recebe alta em São Gonça | G1
articles.standfirst: Valdeci Pereira da Cruz, de 65 anos, contou também foi esfaqueado durante o ataque. Ele passou por cirurgia e ficou internado no CTI do Hospital Estadual Alberto Torres.
articles.summary: O comerciante Valdeci Pereira da Cruz, de 65 anos, recebeu alta do Hospital Estadual Alberto Torres (Heat), em São Gonçalo, na manhã desta segunda-feira (16).
articles.body:
O comerciante Valdeci Pereira da Cruz, de 65 anos, recebeu alta do Hospital Estadual Alberto Torres (Heat), em São Gonçalo , na Região Metropolitana do Rio, na manhã desta segunda-feira (16). Ele foi baleado na cabeça e esfaqueado durante um assalto na última quinta-feira (12).

Valdeci foi abordado por dois homens em uma motocicleta quando abria a oficina mecânica que mantém no bairro Anaia Pequeno.

“Fui entregar um material às 6h, fui abrir a oficina, quando o rapaz perguntou o que tinha para ele. Eu falei que não tinha nada. Ele me mandou sentar em uma cadeira, me deu umas quatro facadas nas costas e, por último, me deu um tiro no ouvido. Eu vi que estava sozinho lá dentro. Saí cambaleando e caí no meio da rua”, contou Valdeci, emocionado.

Vizinhos encontraram o comerciante ferido e o levaram para o Hospital Estadual Alberto Torres. Ele passou por cirurgia e foi encaminhado ao Centro de Tratamento Intensivo (CTI).

Antes de deixar a unidade, Valdeci agradeceu à equipe médica e às pessoas que o ajudaram. Imagens dele foram divulgadas pela Secretaria Estadual de Saúde do Rio de Janeiro .

“Na oficina vocês consertam carro, aqui vocês consertam gente”, disse aos profissionais de saúde.

Valdeci foi atendido no Hospital Estadual Alberto Torres (Heat), em São Gonçalo — Foto: Divulgação/ Secretaria Estadual de Saúde do Rio de Janeiro

Segundo os médicos, apesar da alta, Valdeci ainda corre o risco de perder a audição do ouvido esquerdo.

Esta não foi a primeira internação dele no Hospital Estadual Alberto Torres. O comerciante teve um dos braços amputados após um acidente de carro sofrido anteriormente.

Ao deixar o hospital, Valdeci disse que pretendia reencontrar a família.

“A primeira coisa que vou fazer hoje é dar um beijo nos meus netos, agradecer a Deus por vocês, pela minha vida, e tentar curtir agora, um pouco, com a minha família. Hoje é bênção”, afirmou.

O caso foi registrado na 74ª DP (Alcântara) e será encaminhado à 75ª DP (Rio do Ouro), que ficará responsável pela investigação. Segundo a Polícia Civil , agentes realizam diligências para apurar as circunstâncias do crime.

Vítima foi levada para o Hospital Estadual Alberto Torres — Foto: Reprodução/ TV Globo

articles.title: Motorista envolvido em acidente que matou criança de 10 anos pode responder por homicídio doloso, na Paraíba | G1
articles.standfirst: Delegado Gilson Teles, responsável pela investigação, afirmou que o laudo preliminar da perícia apontou elementos que indicam dolo eventual, como os indícios de embriaguez do motorista e a velocidade acima da permitida na via.
articles.summary: Delegado Gilson Teles, responsável pela investigação, afirmou que o laudo preliminar da perícia apontou elementos que indicam dolo eventual, como os indícios de embriaguez do motorista e a velocidade acima da permitida na via.
articles.body:
O motorista do carro envolvido no acidente que matou uma criança de 10 anos na PB-095, rodovia que liga Massaranduba a Campina Grande , pode responder por homicídio doloso, quando há intenção de matar ou se assume o risco de provocar a morte. Ele foi preso nesta segunda-feira (16). O acidente foi registrado em 12 de outubro. A vítima, Samuel Luccas Rodrigues Araújo, morreu após ser arremessada de uma motocicleta.

Após a prisão do suspeito, o delegado Gilson Teles, responsável pela investigação, afirmou que o laudo preliminar da perícia apontou elementos que indicam dolo eventual, como os indícios de embriaguez do motorista e a velocidade acima da permitida na via.

"O laudo preliminar da perícia foi determinante para entendermos que se tratava de um dolo eventual, porque nós tínhamos, é, sintomas de embriaguez, conforme testemunhas que tiveram contato com o suspeito logo depois do acidente. Nós tivemos uma alta velocidade, acima do que era permitido na via".

Motorista envolvido em acidente que matou criança de 10 anos é preso na Paraíba — Foto: Reprodução Polícia Civil.

De acordo com o Comando de Policiamento de Trânsito (CPTran), com o impacto da colisão, a vítima foi arremessada da moto para o telhado de uma casa às margens da rodovia. A criança morreu no local e o homem que conduzia a moto foi socorrido para Campina Grande.

O piloto da motocicleta segue internado no Hospital de Emergência e Trauma de Campina Grande, com quadro clínico considerado estável.

O motorista do carro envolvido na colisão não prestou socorro às vítimas. Imagens de câmeras de segurança registraram o homem fugindo do local a pé após a omissão do socorro.

No vídeo, que tem cerca de 50 segundos, o homem aparece andando por uma estrada de terra, em uma área próxima a uma mata. Ele caminha sem demonstrar pressa e deixa o local do acidente, onde o carro ficou abandonado.

Em 15 de outubro, o motorista prestou depoimento à Polícia Civil e foi liberado. De acordo com a apuração da TV Paraíba , o homem, que não teve a identidade divulgada, compareceu à Delegacia de Polícia Civil de Massaranduba acompanhado de um advogado.

Na ocasião, a polícia informou que ele seria ouvido novamente mas não confirmou a data.

Moradores cobraram sinalização da rodovia

Em 13 de outubro, moradores da comunidade de Chã do Marinho, entre Campina Grande e Massaranduba, interditaram um trecho da PB-095 para cobrar melhorias na sinalização da rodovia. Durante a manifestação, pneus e outros objetos foram queimados no meio da pista, bloqueando a passagem de veículos nos dois sentidos.

Os manifestantes pediram a instalação de um redutor de velocidade, além de iluminação pública, placas de sinalização e faixa de pedestres.

À TV Paraíba , o Departamento de Estradas de Rodagem da Paraíba (DER-PB) informou que está apurando as informações e que deve enviar um posicionamento sobre as reivindicações dos moradores.

Criança morta após ser arremessada de moto em acidente no Agreste da PB é sepultada em Campina Grande — Foto: Isabella Silva/TV Paraíba

O corpo de Samuel Luccas Rodrigues Araújo, de 10 anos, foi sepultado na tarde de 14 de outubro , no Cemitério São José, no bairro José Pinheiro, em Campina Grande.

O velório de Samuel começou na noite de 13 de outubro, no Grupo Escolar Manuel Sabino de Farias, no Sítio Marinho, próximo ao local do acidente. Em seguida, o corpo foi levado em um cortejo de cerca de 6 quilômetros até Campina Grande, acompanhado por uma cavalgada e por familiares e amigos.

O sepultamento aconteceu por volta das 16h30 do dia 14 de outubro no Cemitério São José, em Campina Grande.

articles.title: Ken Urker’s Cause of Death Confirmed by Louisiana Coroner’s Office
articles.summary: Police have confirmed the cause of death for Ken Urker, the boyfriend of Gypsy Rose Blanchard, who was found dead in a Louisiana home on Oct. 1.
articles.body: Authorities have confirmed that Ken Urker, the boyfriend of Gypsy Rose Blanchard, died from an accidental drug overdose. Urker’s cause of death was listed as “accidental poly substance drug toxicity,” according to a statement on Nov. 16 by the the Lafourche Parish Coroner’s Office in Louisiana. “The case is now complete, and no further testing is pending,” the coroner’s office said in its statement. According to the CDC, a polysubstance drug overdose occurs from exposure to more than one drug. Substances can include stimulants, opioids, counterfeit pills and more. Urker, 34, was found dead on Oct. 1 at a home in Raceland, Louisiana, the Lafourche Parish Sheriff’s Office previously confirmed to NBC News. “We responded to a residence at 107 Double H Drive, Lot 4, in Raceland today after receiving a call at 6:15 p.m.,” the sheriff’s department said in a statement. Authorities said Urker was found “dead upon arrival” and they were investigating the case. On Oct. 2, NBC News obtained a preliminary report from the sheriff’s department that said the death was “drug related.” The report also listed the incident code as “overdose.” At the time, police said they did not find any signs of foul play. Urker shared a 1-year-old daughter, Aurora, with Blanchard, who served eight years in prison for her involvement in the death of her mother. Following reports of his death, Blanchard told People that Urker died of an overdose. “Ken was an amazing father and a man who was deeply loved,” she said. “He will forever be my soulmate and my red string, a connection that time, distance, and even death can never erase.” The two met when Blanchard was in prison. They got engaged in 2018 but later called it quits. Blanchard and Urker reunited a year after she was released from prison in 2023. The preliminary report said Blanchard’s half brother, Dylan Blanchard, and another man named Justin Daigle found Urker the night he died. They told police they entered Urker’s home through an unlocked bedroom window and found him unconscious on his bed. Sister-in-law Anita Blanchard was the one who called the police. According to the report, authorities also discovered syringes and a spoon in the bathroom of the home, as well as “a brown powdery substance.” Another syringe and a handgun were found on the nightstand next to the bed. Additionally, there was a paper towel “with what appeared to be blotches of blood” on Urker’s left arm.

articles.title: 9 Best Fruits That May Help Lower Dementia Risk And Protect Brain Health
articles.summary: Fruit reduces dementia risk by fighting inflammation and protecting brain health. Dietitians recommend eating berries, apples, pears, grapes, citrus and more.
articles.body: Fruit can be a sweet way to reduce your risk of dementia, the devastating loss of memory and cognitive function that can strike older adults. What people eat can play an important role in brain health as they age, says Lisa Young, a registered dietitian and an adjunct professor of nutrition at New York University. “We often think about a healthy diet in terms of protecting the heart, but the brain can benefit too,” Young, the author of “Finally Full, Finally Slim,” tells TODAY.com. “The brain relies on a steady supply of nutrients, and what we eat can influence inflammation, oxidative stress, blood vessel health and other processes involved in cognitive function.” Research suggests certain dietary patterns — such as the Mediterranean diet, which prioritizes fruits and vegetables, whole grains, beans, nuts, olive oil and fish — may be linked with a lower risk of dementia, she adds. Eating lots of flavonoid-rich fruits in midlife was “significantly associated” with a 44% decreased risk of dementia from any cause, researchers reported in the Journal of Prevention of Alzheimer’s Disease. Flavonoids are naturally occurring plant compounds found in many fruits and other plant foods, Young says. They help give some fruits their vibrant colors and have antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, she adds. Their benefits for cognition include protecting neurons from neurotoxins and fighting inflammation of brain tissue, plus improving blood flow to the brain, the study noted. A diet high in flavonoids from fruits and other foods was associated with lower odds of cognitive decline, according to a separate paper published in Neurology. The findings “support a benefit of higher flavonoid intakes for maintaining cognitive function,” the authors wrote. People who ate plenty of foods rich in flavonoids, such as berries and apples, were less likely to develop Alzheimer’s disease than those who ate few of those foods, another study found. Certain fruits are an “excellent source” of flavonoids, Young says. She encourages people to eat a variety of colorful plant foods to get different types of flavonoids, plus fiber, vitamins, minerals and other beneficial compounds. Here are nine fruits to consider when aiming to reduce dementia risk: Apples This classic fruit is a “very significant source of flavonoids” in the U.S. diet, researchers note. The skin contains these and other beneficial plant compounds, plus lots of fiber, so it’s best not to peel your apples when you eat them, Young advises. Apples are also among the best fruits to reduce heart disease risk. Pears Juicy, sweet and rich in fiber, pears make the list of the healthiest fall foods. Similar to apples, the peel holds lots of flavonoids and many other nutrients, so aim to eat pears with the skin on. Oranges Citrus flavonoids exhibit “anti-aging activities,” researchers note. In oranges, a type of flavonoid called hesperidin suppresses inflammation and has been linked to cognitive function, says registered dietitian Natalie Rizzo, nutrition editor for TODAY. “The majority of the hesperidin in oranges is found in the peel. Since a whole orange (including the peel) is squeezed to make a glass of OJ, hesperidin is most abundant in orange juice,” she notes. Grapefruit Frequent consumption of citrus fruits including grapefruit is associated with a lower risk of dementia, a study found. Naringin, a flavonoid subtype, is abundant in citrus fruits, particularly grapefruit, researchers note. It’s being investigated as a potential “therapeutic agent” for Alzheimer’s disease. As you enjoy grapefruit, keep in mind that it can interact with some medications. Berries Blueberries and strawberries are particularly good choices when it comes to fruits that may lower dementia risk, Young says. Frozen berries are as nutritious as the fresh option, she adds. “Freezing generally preserves many of the beneficial plant compounds in berries, including flavonoids, and frozen fruit can be a convenient and economical way to enjoy them year-round,” Young notes. “I recommend buying unsweetened frozen berries and adding them to oatmeal, yogurt or smoothies, or enjoying them on their own. Fresh and frozen berries are both nutritious options, so choose whichever you are more likely to eat regularly.” Registered dietitian Samantha Cassetty considers blueberries the healthiest berry and the healthiest fruit overall. TODAY nutrition and health expert Joy Bauer advises eating 2 cups or more of berries per week. Peaches Compounds in peach flesh and peach peels can decrease the risk of brain disorders because of their antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effect, studies note. Frozen peaches are a good alternative once the fresh fruit is out of season. Apricots The bright orange fruits have a high polyphenol content and show “moderate neuroprotective potential,” studies have shown. If you prefer dried apricots, be aware that drying can change the levels of individual plant compounds, so dried and fresh fruit aren’t necessarily identical nutritionally, Young notes. She recommends enjoying dried fruit in moderate portions, ideally without added sugar. Plums The fruit’s deeply purple or red skin signals the presence of powerful antioxidants. Plums are rich in flavonoids, and research about their health benefits shows promising results when it comes to their “memory-improving characteristics,” a systematic review found. Plum consumption was also associated with improved cognitive function. Prunes, the dried version of plums, were used in many of the studies in the review. Grapes Red grapes are loaded with flavonoids, Julia Zumpano, a registered dietitian with the Cleveland Clinic’s Center for Human Nutrition, previously told TODAY.com. Grapes show “promising results” for their positive effects on cognitive function and can enhance some aspects of cognition, a systematic review of randomized controlled trials found. Grapes also make the list of fruits that can help reduce the risk of cancer.

articles.title: Widely used antidepressant outperformed by 3 other drugs in major study of 30,000 people
articles.summary: A study of 20 antidepressants and over 30,000 patients found three medications may beat fluoxetine for long-term depression treatment results overall.
articles.body: Three antidepressants may work better than fluoxetine, widely known by the brand name Prozac, at helping people with depression get better and stay well over time, a new study suggests. The research, published in The Lancet Psychiatry, compared 20 antidepressants to determine how well they eased depression symptoms and helped prevent them from returning over time. Researchers analyzed 115 previous clinical trials involving more than 30,000 people, according to a news release from Radboud University Medical Center in the Netherlands. CERTAIN SLEEP HABITS COULD OFFER CLUES TO HIDDEN TYPE OF DEPRESSION, SCIENTISTS SAY They found that escitalopram, sold under the brand name Lexapro; duloxetine, sold as Cymbalta; and agomelatine performed better over the long term than fluoxetine, which researchers used as the main comparison drug. Eli Lilly told Fox News Digital that it discontinued manufacturing Prozac in 2024. The company noted that fluoxetine remains available in many FDA-approved generic medicines and that neither the study nor the university’s news release specifically referred to Prozac or any Lilly product. The findings suggest that antidepressants can continue helping people after their symptoms improve, although some medications appeared to work better than others at keeping patients well. Paul van Haaren, a researcher at Radboud University Medical Center who worked on the study, noted that the three medications have different benefits and drawbacks. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "Escitalopram is already widely used," he said in the release. "Agomelatine works well, but one of its side effects is the risk of liver failure. Duloxetine is less well-known and is prescribed less frequently as a first-line treatment." Escitalopram belongs to a common group of antidepressants known as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs. These medications are often recommended as a first option for treating depression, according to the release. Among the SSRIs included in the study, escitalopram appeared to work best at helping patients stay well over time. Eric Ruhé, a professor of difficult-to-treat depression at Radboud University Medical Center, said the findings could eventually influence how doctors choose antidepressants. Still, the researchers stressed that this does not mean everyone with depression should take escitalopram. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "As a prescriber, you consider the balance between a medication's benefits and side effects," Ruhé said in the release. "That balance differs from person to person." Dr. Carole Lieberman, a board-certified psychiatrist based in Beverly Hills, California, who was not involved in the study, urged caution when interpreting the findings. She noted that agomelatine is not approved in the U.S. "The best way to treat someone with depression is not always with antidepressants, and certainly not with antidepressants alone," Lieberman told Fox News Digital. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Psychotherapy or talk therapy can also play an important role in treating depression, according to Lieberman, while some patients may benefit from using medication along with therapy. There were some limitations to the study, the researchers acknowledged. Rather than enrolling a new group of patients and following them over time, the researchers combined results from 115 previous clinical trials to compare how the medications performed. The findings also cannot predict which antidepressant will work best for a specific person. The researchers stressed that doctors and patients should consider both the potential benefits and side effects when choosing a medication. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP People with questions about their antidepressants should speak with their doctor before making any medication changes, according to the release. Fox News Digital reached out to the researchers and additional drug manufacturers for comment.

articles.title: The No. 1 Consideration When Picking the Healthiest Cutting Board Material, According to Experts
articles.summary: Cutting boards can be made from wood, plastic, silicone or glass. Does the material matter for your health, and which type of cutting board is safest? Food safety experts weigh in.
articles.body: Cutting boards are kitchen staples that come into contact with many of the foods we cook and eat. They serve as a crucial barrier between countertops and sharp knives, and provide a clean, sturdy surface to prepare foods. These days, you can find a wide array of cutting boards made from different materials. These include hardwood, plastic, silicone or stainless steel. Most chefs have strong opinions about the best type of cutting board. But what about the health effects? Does the material make a difference for your health, and is one safest to use? Maybe you’re wondering whether certain cutting boards harbor more bacteria, or you’re concerned about microplastics. We asked experts which type of cutting board is best from a health and food safety standpoint, and here’s what they had to say. What Is the Healthiest Cutting Board To Use? Many experts prefer using hardwood or plastic cutting boards, which are both healthy and safe for everyday use, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. “I’d say pick whatever one you have a preference for. There is no one ‘healthier’ one. Each of them has trade offs,” Ben Chapman, Ph.D., head of the Department of Agricultural and Human Sciences at North Carolina State University, tells TODAY.com. Traditionally, cutting boards were made from wood. At some point around the 1950s, people began switching to plastic. “A lot of people were concerned about the ability to clean and sanitize wood cutting boards,” says Chapman. Plastic was thought to be more sanitary because wood is porous and harder to clean. In a landmark 1994 study, researchers at the University of California, Davis tested this theory by applying pathogens to different types of cutting boards and measuring what was left after cleaning them. Surprisingly, they found that plastic wasn’t more hygienic— in fact, less bacteria survived on the surface of wood cutting boards. That’s because the fibers of the wood absorb water along with any bacteria, which gets trapped beneath the surface of the board and killed off as the wood dries, Chapman explains. However, all cutting boards have drawbacks, and some experts argue that the material is less about your health than it is about your cutting board habits. “It really depends on how you’re using it, how you’re cleaning it,” Wade Syers, a food safety specialist with Michigan State University Extension, tells TODAY.com. Here are the pros and cons of each cutting board material: Wood Wood cutting boards are a top choice among food safety experts. There are different types of wood cutting boards, including solid hardwood, like maple and walnut and bamboo. “There’s no difference from a safety standpoint,” says Chapman. Wood is more flexible than plastic because the fibers bend and give under the pressure of a knife, the experts note. The harder the wood, the more resistant it is to deep scratches and scarring. The main downside of wood cutting boards is that they’re more difficult to clean and sanitize, the experts say. “And drying them well really, really matters,” says Chapman. Wood cutting boards are not dishwasher-safe because the high temperatures can damage the wood. The best way to clean them is by hand-washing the boards with hot water and soap and letting the wood air-dry completely, the experts note. It’s also important to sanitize the wood, says Syers, which will kill any lingering pathogens. The USDA recommends using a diluted bleach solution made with one tablespoon of chlorine bleach per gallon of water. Pour this onto the wood board and wait several minutes before rinsing it off, then allow it to dry. “Anything that’s left on the outside you haven’t killed is going to get sucked inside the wood (as it dries),” says Chapman. Wood cutting boards do require some upkeep. You can refresh the wood by sanding down rough, scratched layers and treating the wood with mineral oil, says Chapman. Plastic Plastic cutting boards are also a popular choice among experts. These are typically made from polypropylene or polyethylene, which are lightweight and non-porous. “From a cleaning standpoint, plastic is easier,” says Syers. Chapman prefers using plastic cutting boards for raw meat and poultry, because they can go straight in the dishwasher. The washing cycle will clean the board thoroughly. “The heat generated through the sanitizing cycle is certainly enough to kill any pathogen that might be there,” says Chapman. The main issue with plastic is the way it gets worn down by knives. Unlike wood, plastic is less flexible and develops very deep grooves and scratches, says Chapman. “It’s a place to hold food debris, as well as bacteria, and yeast and mold that could survive the sanitizing process in the dishwasher because mold spores are heat-tolerant,” Chapman adds. Another concern is that plastic boards can release microplastics into food. However, both experts agree that the research on the health effects of ingesting microplastics is still emerging, and more human studies are needed. “I don’t think we have enough science right now to know what the impacts are,” says Chapman. If you’re concerned about microplastics, you can use another cutting board material instead. “It’s based on how you weigh those pros and cons,” says Syers. Silicone Silicone is a non-toxic, plastic-free alternative to rigid plastic cutting boards. These boards or mats are non-porous, so they won’t absorb moisture or pathogens. Silicone can withstand high temperatures, so it can be cleaned in the dishwasher. The material is much more flexible and soft than regular plastic boards. However, that also makes it prone to damage from knives. Cuts, tears and scratches in the silicone can also harbor food debris and bacteria or mold, says Chapman. These may need to be replaced more frequently, and aren’t ideal for heavy-duty chopping. Metal, Glass or Marble You can also find solid, non-porous cutting boards made from glass, stainless steel, marble or stone. These are very easy to clean and sanitize, says Syers, but have several downsides. First, they’re heavy and harder to use because of their slick, slippery surface — this can increase the risk of knife accidents. Materials like glass or marble may break or chip more easily. “They’re also really, really hard on knives,” says Syers. Over time, these can dull blades and make them less functional. These generally aren’t recommended for everyday food prep, the experts note. Which Cutting Board Is Safest for Raw Meats? Wood and plastic cutting boards are both safe to use to cut raw meat and poultry, per the USDA. Raw meats carry a higher risk of spreading food-borne pathogens, including salmonella and E. coli. That’s why any cutting board that comes into contact with raw meat needs to be cleaned and sanitized, especially before it’s used to cut food that won’t get cooked, like fresh produce. “I think the biggest food safety concern with regard to cutting boards is the chance to cross-contaminate food,” says Syers. Many experts prefer to use plastic cutting boards for raw meats — not because the plastic is safer, says Chapman, but because it’s easier to sanitize in the dishwasher. However, wood may have natural antimicrobial properties and is a good option for raw meats as long as you clean and sanitize it properly between uses. Syers prefers to use two designated cutting boards for different purposes: plastic for raw meats and a wooden board for produce, bread and everything else. “It just adds one more layer of food safety to help avoid that cross-contamination,” says Syers. When To Replace Cutting Boards Between all the chopping, dicing and mincing, cutting boards will get worn out over time and need to be replaced. Wood cutting boards can last for decades if you care for them properly, the experts note. However, if the wood develops deep cracks, splinters or has signs of mold growth, it’s time to toss it out. Plastic boards have a shorter lifespan, usually around one to three years if you use them regularly, the experts note. Once the plastic develops deep grooves or scratches and has discoloration after cleaning, it’s time to replace the board, says Chapman. “We don’t want those pathogens to have any place to hide when we’re cleaning the boards,” Syers adds.

articles.title: More than 100 pregnant women confirmed to have measles, new report finds
articles.summary: For the first time in decades, U.S. doctors are sounding the alarm about babies coming into the world with measles.
articles.body: For the first time in decades, U.S. doctors are sounding the alarm about babies coming into the world with measles. Congenital measles happens when a pregnant woman passes the virus to her fetus in the womb. It can lead to serious complications or even be deadly for newborns. From the start of 2025 through the end of this September, 13 congenital measles cases were reported to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention during large measles outbreaks, according to preliminary figures published in a medical journal on Monday. “This is a brand new phenomenon,” said Michael Osterholm, who directs the University of Minnesota’s Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy. The condition’s emergence is driven by declining vaccination rates, which have fueled the virus’s spread so much that the Pan American Health Organization is expected to officially announce Tuesday that the U.S. has lost the measles-free status it’s had since 2000. In the past two years, according to the CDC, there have been more than 7,500 measles cases. “We’re now seeing levels of measles that we haven’t seen in 30 years,” said Dr. Adam Ratner, a member of the American Academy of Pediatrics’ infectious diseases committee. “When you have measles under control,” congenital measles doesn’t happen. The preliminary case figures were released in a public health alert published by NEJM Evidence in partnership with the center Osterholm directs. The alert also said there were 112 cases of confirmed measles during pregnancy — almost all among women who didn’t get vaccinated against measles beforehand or whose vaccination status was unknown. The alert said getting vaccinated before pregnancy and having high vaccination rates in the community “are important to prevent measles and related complications.” CDC scientists authored the alert. Guidance on congenital measles from the pediatrics academy is already reaching doctors. And Pennsylvania’s health department published an advisory last month for healthcare providers, schools, childcare centers and others in the state, which currently has the largest measles outbreak in the nation. A new reality allows congenital measles to emerge People gain immunity to measles by getting the disease or the vaccine. Before the shots existed, lots of people were infected by the extremely contagious virus in childhood. Later, high vaccination rates protected everyone. But a new and historic reality — shaped both by the success of the vaccine and recent skepticism about it — has triggered congenital measles. “What’s happening is we have so many women of childbearing age who were not vaccinated in the last 25 years, nor have they ever had exposure to measles because for the last 25 years we have beaten it back,” Osterholm said. “Now, this group is highly susceptible to measles.” Doctors say the best way to prevent the disease is for women to get the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, known as MMR, before pregnancy. This protects the fetus too because antibodies pass from mother to baby through the placenta. Protection can last a few months after birth. MMR can’t be given during pregnancy. Unvaccinated women who have never had measles and are exposed while pregnant can get a solution containing antibodies within six days to reduce the risk of infection and complications. Congenital measles can seriously harm babies If a woman gets measles toward the end of pregnancy, there’s a good chance she will pass it along. An estimated 25% to 30% of babies born to someone who gets measles shortly before delivery may become infected, the pediatrics group says. Babies are considered to have congenital measles if they were exposed in the uterus and doctors find evidence of measles very soon after birth. Common symptoms include fever, jaundice and a measles rash. Severe complications include pneumonia, encephalitis and a rare condition known as SSPE, a brain disorder that generally develops many years after a measles infection and is almost always fatal. Ratner, who wrote a book about measles, said there are indications that kids with congenital measles are at higher risk for SSPE and may develop it sooner after having measles than other children. “That’s something that sadly we’re learning more about,” he said. Doctors worry things may get worse if vaccination rates keep dropping. Outbreaks are considered unlikely if a community has a 95% MMR rate, but rates in many communities have dipped below that threshold. Nationally, the CDC said, 92.4% of U.S. kindergarteners in 2025-26 received required MMR shots. This puts many vulnerable people at risk, including infants too young to be vaccinated. The first MMR dose is routinely given at 12 to 15 months old, and the earliest babies can get the shots is 6 months in outbreak areas. “We need to get back to the point where everybody who can get vaccinated is getting vaccinated, and that’s gonna take some doing,” Ratner said. “It’s going to be a lot of work on the part of pediatricians and public health institutions and lots of others. But it’s an important thing for us to do.”

articles.title: Família é resgata de telhado após casa ficar submersa em temporal  | G1
articles.standfirst: Todo o estado está com avisos meteorológicos de temporal, conforme divulgado pelo Inmet. Há registros de alagamentos e desabamentos no interior.
articles.summary: Todo o estado está com avisos meteorológicos de temporal, conforme divulgado pelo Inmet. Há registros de alagamentos e desabamentos no interior.
articles.body:
Um vídeo mostra o momento em que uma família foi resgatada do telhado da casa em que morava, em Malhada , no sudoeste da Bahia, após as fortes chuvas que atingem a cidade deixar o imóvel praticamente submerso. O resgate aconteceu na segunda-feira (16), em uma comunidade rural.

Segundo a Defesa Civil, a cidade registrou 240 mm de chuva e é uma dos 19 municípios em estado de emergência por causa das chuvas.

Na filmagem, é possível ver que um homem, uma mulher e duas crianças esperavam resgate em cima do telhado. Eles foram retirados do local por outros moradores da comunidade, que chegaram até o imóvel com um barco.

Além dos alagamentos, as ruas da cidade ficaram completamente destruídas, e casas e carros foram danificados.

Veja fotos da cidade nesta terça-feira (17):

A Superintendência de Proteção e Defesa Civil (Sudec) acompanha os procedimentos relacionados à situação de emergência e mantém preparada a ajuda humanitária, com colchões, lençóis, cobertores e kits de higiene pessoal e doméstica.

Segundo o Governo do Estado, o programa Bahia Sem Fome vai enviar 300 cestas alimentares para a cidade. A Secretaria de Assistência e Desenvolvimento Social (Seades) atua na identificação das famílias afetadas, na avaliação do acesso ao aluguel social e no atendimento alimentar.

Em Jequié , também no sudoeste do estado, caminhões ficaram submersos pela água na noite de segunda-feira.

Na cidade de Nova Canaã , no interior do estado, o telhado do Hospital Municipal desabou e 10 pessoas precisaram ser transferidas para uma unidade de saúde de outra cidade.

Assim como Malhada , o município também foi incluído na lista de cidades em situação de emergência. Veja lista das cidades:

Todas as regiões da Bahia estão com avisos meteorológicos de tempestade nesta terça-feira, de acordo com o Instituto Nacional de Meteorologia (Inmet). De acordo com o órgão, os avisos são válidos até 23h59.

Todas as cidades, incluindo Salvador, estão sob alerta amarelo, que indica perigo potencial. Em parte do sul, sudoeste e oeste baiano, o grau de severidade do aviso indica perigo.

🟡 Em todo o estado, há risco de chuvas de até 50 mm durante o dia, ventos de até 60 km/h e queda de granizo.

🟠 Em cidades do sul, sudoeste e oeste da Bahia, o risco é ainda maior: pode chover 100 mm, os ventos podem chegar a 100 km/h e há risco de queda de granizo, corte de energia, alagamentos, queda de árvores e desabamentos

articles.title: Carreta dá 'L', atinge carro e deixa quatro feridos na BR-101 no ES | G1
articles.standfirst: Veículo de carga invadiu a contramão no quilômetro 234, na altura de Fundão. Condutor da carreta não sofreu ferimentos.
articles.summary: Veículo de carga invadiu a contramão no quilômetro 234, na altura de Fundão. Condutor da carreta não sofreu ferimentos.
articles.body:
Acidente entre carreta e carro da Prefeitura de Rio Bananal deixou quatro feridos na BR-101, no Espírito Santo — Foto: Divulgação/PRF

Um acidente envolvendo uma carreta e um carro de passeio deixou quatro pessoas feridas e interditou o quilômetro 234 da BR-101, em Fundão , no Espírito Santo, por volta das 7h desta terça-feira (17).

A Ecovias Capixaba, concessionária responsável pelo trecho, informou que o trânsito foi liberado por volta de 8h50.

Agentes da Polícia Rodoviária Federal (PRF) que atuaram na ocorrência informaram que a carreta fez uma manobra em 'L', invadiu a contramão e atingiu o carro, que pertence à prefeitura de Rio Bananal , no Norte do estado.

Todos os feridos estavam no carro e foram socorridos com ferimentos de média gravidade. O condutor da carreta, que carregava um contêiner vazio, não sofreu ferimentos.

A Ecovias Capixaba informou que a ocorrência segue em andamento. O motorista da carreta foi submetido ao teste do bafômetro, que deu negativo.

Feridos estavam a caminho de seminário, diz prefeitura

Procurada pelo g1 , a Prefeitura de Rio Bananal informou que o veículo envolvido no acidente pertence a Secretaria Municipal de Assistência Social e seguia com destino a Vitória.

No carro, estavam quatro servidores municipais, um motorista do sexo masculino e três servidoras do sexo feminino, que participariam de um seminário.

Ainda de acordo com a administração municipal, duas servidoras que estavam no banco traseiro ficaram feridas e foram levadas de ambulância para um hospital em Aracruz. Já o motorista e a servidora que estava no banco do passageiro foram transferidos para o Hospital Estadual Dr. Jayme Santos Neves, na Serra.

Não foram divulgadas informações detalhadas sobre o estado de saúde dos envolvidos.

“A Prefeitura de Rio Bananal acompanha a situação e aguarda novas informações das equipes responsáveis. Novas atualizações serão divulgadas assim que houver informações oficiais e confirmadas”, finalizou a prefeitura, em nota oficial.

articles.title: Homem esfaqueia namorada durante jogo de baralho em SP | G1
articles.standfirst: Thiago Rodrigues dos Santos foi encontrado depois do ataque, armado com uma faca, em Catanduva (SP) na segunda-feira (16). Na delegacia, também resistiu à prisão, feriu um policial civil e arrancou o banco da cela.
articles.summary: Thiago Rodrigues dos Santos foi preso em flagrante após atacar a vítima por ciúmes; ele ainda feriu um policial e danificou a delegacia durante a ocorrência.
articles.body:
Thiago Rodrigues dos Santos foi preso em Catanduva (SP) — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

Uma mulher foi esfaqueada duas vezes no peito pelo namorado no bairro Residencial Nova Catanduva , na segunda-feira (16), em Catanduva (SP). O suspeito do crime, Thiago Rodrigues dos Santos, foi preso em flagrante.

Thiago Rodrigues dos Santos é o suspeito do crime. Ele fugiu, mas foi localizado pela polícia atrás de um comércio na rodovia, armado com uma faca e preso em flagrante por tentativa de feminicídio, violência doméstica, lesão corporal e resistência.

Segundo o boletim de ocorrência, a vítima esfaqueada foi levada ao Hospital Padre Albino consciente. Na unidade, ela disse à polícia que jogava baralho com ele, quando ele começou a ficar violento e a beber. A mulher contou que Thiago pegou uma faca na cozinha e a esfaqueou.

Ela conseguiu escapar e pediu ajuda aos vizinhos que acionaram o resgate. A mulher pediu medidas protetivas de urgência contra o namorado.

Na delegacia, Thiago precisou ser algemado. Ele confessou o crime, motivado por ciúmes. De acordo com o registro policial, durante os procedimentos, ele começou a socar as grades e a se jogar contra a estrutura da cela, até arrancar o assento instalado no local.

Um policial chegou a ficar ferido nas mãos e nos braços enquanto tentava conter o suspeito.

articles.title: Jovem revela que pulou de carro em movimento ao ser espancada | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo ela, os dois se conheceram há cerca de uma semana antes do crime. Além das agressões, Lucas San Thiago Batista Moreira teria dito que iria matar a mãe e as filhas da vítima.
articles.summary: Segundo ela, os dois se conheceram há cerca de uma semana antes do crime. Além das agressões, Lucas San Thiago Batista Moreira teria dito que iria matar a mãe e as filhas da vítima
articles.body:
Uma mulher de 28 anos precisou pular de um carro em movimento ao ser espancada com uma série de socos, segundo o que foi relatado por ela à Guarda Civil Municipal de Goiânia . A jovem e o suspeito, Lucas San Thiago Batista Moreira, teriam discutido em um motel e, em seguida, ele teria começado as agressões dentro do carro, quando a levava para casa. O caso é investigado como ameaça e lesão corporal, no contexto de violência doméstica.

O homem foi localizado no setor sudoeste pela Guarda Civil Municipal, que levou o suspeito à Delegacia Estadual de Atendimento Especializado à Mulher (Deaem). Ele passou por audiência de custódia e teve a prisão em flagrante convertida em preventiva.

Em nota, a Defensoria Pública do Estado de Goiás informou que representou o investigado durante a audiência de custódia, cumprindo seu dever legal e constitucional de garantir a defesa de pessoas que não tenham condições de pagar por um profissional particular, e não comentará sobre o caso.

O crime aconteceu no domingo (15). De acordo com a jovem, os dois estavam saindo de um motel e Lucas apresentava um comportamento agressivo. Dentro do carro, ele teria começado a falar sobre o crime organizado, momento em que as agressões começaram.

"Muitos socos, um atrás do outro. [...] Antes de eu pular, enquanto ele me dava socos, ele falava o tempo todo que eu ia morrer", disse ele em um relato exibido pela TV Anhanguera.

Às autoridades, ela contou que ele começou a agredi-la fisicamente, desferindo diversos socos em seu rosto e cabeça. Disse ainda que ele desferia diversos socos enquanto a ameaçava de morte e que, durante as agressões, Lucas afirmou expressamente: "Você vai morrer, desgraçada, eu vou te matar".

Jovem revela que pulou de carro em movimento ao ser espancada com série de socos — Foto: Reprodução/TV Anhanguera e Divulgação/GCM

A jovem conta ainda que, em determinado momento, o homem teria dito que pararia o carro e pegaria um pedaço de madeira para lhe dar pauladas. Neste momento, ela conta que estava próximo de desmaiar e que ficou com medo de que ele a matasse e, por isso, pulou do carro.

"Destravou o cinto de segurança e, aproveitando-se de um momento de distração de Lucas, puxou a maçaneta e saltou do veículo em movimento, tendo ele ainda tentado segurá-la. Após conseguir sair, levantou-se rapidamente e correu sem olhar para trás, temendo que Lucas retornasse ou passasse com o veículo por cima dela", diz o relato.

Um motociclista que passava pelo local ajudou a jovem. O Serviço de Atendimento Móvel de Urgência (Samu) encaminhou a vítima para o CAIS de Campinas. Posteriormente, ela foi transferida para o Hospital de Urgências de Goiânia (Hugo) e recebeu alta, segundo a TV Anhanguera.

De acordo com o relato da vítima, ela e Lucas se conheceram cerca de uma semana antes das agressões.

Naquela noite, os dois estavam um um motel, quando o suspeito teria ligado o som em um volume alto, fazendo com que a jovem pedisse que ele repetisse o que falava. "Após permanecerem juntos, percebeu que Lucas estava muito agitado, inquieto, tremendo e mexendo constantemente no telefone celular, além de colocar músicas em volume muito alto" , diz o relato.

Diante disso, ele teria passado a apresentar um comportamento agressivo e acusou de estar zombando dele. Quando saíram do motel, ele teria dito que "conhecer como era lidar com um bandido", além de dizer que já a conhecia, que havia "rastreado" toda a vida dela.

Jovem revela que pulou de carro em movimento ao ser espancada com série de socos — Foto: Divulgação/GCM

O suspeito teria começado a falar sobre o crime organizado e outras coisas "sem sentido", quando a jovem pediu que ele a levasse para casa.

"Na sequência, Lucas passou a dizer que ela estava pedindo pelo amor de Deus da mesma maneira que determinada pessoa teria pedido antes de morrer, momento em que começou a agredi-la fisicamente", disse ela à polícia.

Além disso, ele teria dito que ela teria suas semanas para sair de Goiânia, caso contrário ele mataria a jovem, a mãe e as duas filhas dela. Além de manter o suspeito preso após audiência de custódia

Segundo a Guarda Civil Municipal, Lucas tem antecedentes criminais relacionados ao tráfico de drogas e outras ocorrências. Em outubro do ano passado, uma jovem de 24 anos denunciou ter sido espancada por Lucas, que teria provocado uma batida de carro , causando uma morte deixando seis pessoas feridas.

"Ele está me batendo e me trancando nesse apartamento, eu quero ir embora, estou com medo dele fazer alguma coisa pior”, relatou a jovem em depoimento colhido à época, segundo o documento de medida protetiva, concedida pela Justiça.

Ainda segundo a GCM, há registros de supostas agressões contra policiais penais durante o período em que ele esteve preso. De acordo com o advogado Ricardo Namathallah, que representa Lucas no processo envolvendo o acidente, o processo está suspenso, aguardando o julgamento do incidente de insanidade mental.

articles.title: U.S. loses measles-elimination status, erasing decades of progress
articles.summary: Measles is no longer eliminated in the U.S., a United Nations commission determined, reversing one of the country’s greatest public health achievements this century.
articles.body: Measles is no longer eliminated in the United States, reversing one of the country’s greatest public health achievements this century. An independent commission of the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a group within the World Health Organization, revoked the U.S.’s measles-elimination status, according to sources familiar with the vote, after determining that the virus has circulated nonstop for more than a year. The U.S. earned the designation in 2000. Now, measles is once again endemic. PAHO is expected to officially announce its decision on Tuesday. “The United States has an extraordinary measles problem. We’ve had more measles cases in the last 18 months than we’ve had in the previous 25 years combined,” said Noel Brewer, a public health professor at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Upwards of 5,400 cases have been recorded this year — more than double last year’s count and the highest since 1991. Ten people have died, according to state health departments. PAHO determines whether countries in the Americas meet the requirements for measles elimination. The group deliberated for four days last week in Washington, D.C., to assess whether transmission in the U.S. had been sustained for at least 12 months. A commission made up of eight public health experts evaluated genetic data from “homegrown” cases (those not related to international travel) to figure out whether outbreaks across states were linked. The commission also weighed the level of vaccination coverage in the U.S., the quality of measles surveillance and whether the U.S. has a strategy and resources to respond to outbreaks. As in many countries, vaccination rates in the U.S. have declined in recent years: 92% of kindergarteners had been vaccinated for measles as of the 2025-26 school year, down from 95% — the threshold needed to prevent outbreaks — in the 2019-20 school year. Nationwide among kindergarteners, 75% of counties and jurisdictions with measles vaccine data fall below the 95% rate, according to an NBC News investigation. Endemic measles poses a serious risk to people who are unvaccinated, said Walter Orenstein, former director of the U.S. Immunization Program at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The risk is especially pronounced for infants, who are not typically eligible for the first dose of the vaccine until they turn 1, as well as those who cannot get the shot because they are immunocompromised. “People can go into a supermarket and get infected,” he said. At least four of the measles deaths this year were in babies too young to be vaccinated. Some health departments in outbreak zones are now recommending an early dose for infants as young as 6 months. Measles is among the most contagious viruses known to humans: One infected person can spread the virus to 9 out of 10 others in close proximity. It can linger in the air for up to two hours. Infections in unvaccinated people can lead to deadly complications like pneumonia or swelling of the brain. Brewer said the U.S. desperately needs a strategy for tackling measles. “The lack of action to address the growing outbreak is clear negligence,” he said. Under past presidential administrations, the CDC has responded to measles outbreaks with media briefings and vaccination campaigns, but the agency has not done so this year. A spokesperson for the Health and Human Services Department said the CDC has “mounted an aggressive response to measles outbreaks,” including allocating $100 million in additional funding in October and deploying experts to support state responses. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz “continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles,” the spokesperson said. “We know where transmission is occurring and we’re working with state and local health departments to reach those communities,” Schwartz said in a separate statement. “Losing a designation doesn’t mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks.” Since taking office, Kennedy has questioned the safety and effectiveness of measles vaccines and touted unproven remedies like inhaled steroids. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, falsely suggested in August that the combined measles shot could be “quite lethal,” despite decades of evidence demonstrating its safety. “We have seen frequent and damaging public comments that have been shaking the confidence of parents about vaccination,” Brewer said. Since 2019, 82% of counties and jurisdictions across the U.S. have reported declines in measles vaccination rates. Three small, rural counties — Catron County, New Mexico, and Adams and Custer counties in Idaho — have rates for kindergarteners below 50%. The pandemic accelerated the downward vaccination trend. Some parents avoided taking their children to the pediatrician, which meant delaying routine shots. An onslaught of misinformation about the Covid vaccines also reignited debunked theories, including the false notion that measles shots are linked to autism. Even before the pandemic, the World Health Organization warned that vaccine hesitancy was contributing to a global resurgence of measles. “It’s not just a U.S. problem, and it’s not just this administration,” Brewer said. Last year, Canada’s status was revoked following an outbreak that led to more than 5,000 cases. “It wasn’t for a lack of effort in Canada. There was a political commitment at the highest level to sustain measles elimination and to stop that outbreak. That was for me the sad part of the story, because they really did try,” said Jon Andrus, a global health professor at George Washington University and the chair of the PAHO commission that determines measles elimination status. It could take years, experts say, for the U.S. to reclaim that designation.

articles.title: Royal College of Nursing 'dissatisifed' with safe staffing legislation
articles.summary: Health Minister Robbie Butler introduced the Health and Social Care (Staffing) bill in the assembly on Monday.
articles.body:
The Royal College of Nursing has said it is "extremely dissatisfied" with proposed legislation to strengthen safe staffing across health and social care services in Northern Ireland.

Health minister Robbie Butler introduced the Health and Social Care (Staffing) bill in the assembly on Monday, saying it marked a "significant step".

But a letter to the department from the RCN's director Rita Devlin, seen by BBC News NI, spelled out the nursing union's concerns with the legislation.

There are already laws in Scotland and Wales that place legal duties on NHS trusts to calculate and maintain safe staffing levels.

The Stormont bill aims to strengthen how the health service plans its workforce, identifies staffing risks and ensures appropriately qualified staff are available to deliver safe and effective care.

If passed, it would place workforce planning requirements on a statutory footing, creating formal responsibilities for the Department of Health and individual health trusts.

But Devlin said she did not believe it "adequately reflects" the co-design processes the union had been engaging with the department on since 2020.

She criticised the draft bill for "seeming to imagine that responsibility for workforce planning can somehow be delegated" to the trusts.

Devlin went on to say: "The fact that safe staffing does not appear in the title, or indeed in the bill itself, is of great concern and disappointment to us.

"Workforce planning is a means to an end [the end being the delivery of safe and effective health and social care] it is not an end in itself."

She also described as a "glaring omission" by the department the lack of guiding principles around workforce planning to inform the legislation.

"The absence of these makes the rest of the legislation totally open to interpretation," she added.

She concluded that in the absence of detail the RCN had hoped for, the union was faced with being in the "regrettable position" of lobbying for amendments to the bill.

Devlin said her union believes that all accountability and responsibility for workforce planning must reside "solely" within the department of health.

The proposed changes come amid continuing pressures on health and social care services, with growing demand and workforce challenges affecting patients' needs.

Introducing the bill on Monday, Butler said it represented a "significant step forward in strengthening workforce planning and staffing governance across our health and social care system".

"It places safe and effective staffing at the heart of strategic decision-making and creates a clear legislative framework to support both those who deliver care and those who rely on it."

He added: "This legislation is designed to help create a more sustainable system by ensuring staffing considerations are embedded in planning, delivery and accountability arrangements across health and social care, helping organisations better plan for the workforce needed to meet the changing needs of the population."

However, the Alliance Party's Nuala McAllister, who sits on Stormont's health committee, accused Ulster Unionist health ministers of "wasting six years producing a bill that will make little-to-no difference to safe staffing levels in our hospital wards".

She added: "Grand promises were made about this legislation and it is reprehensible that the evidence-based proposals from frontline health leaders have been thrown in the bin in favour of vague and meaningless commitments from the minister."

She said Alliance would work with health unions to bring forward amendments to the bill "to ensure it delivers the protections staff have been crying out for years".

articles.title: Bystander suffers knife injury during train fight between two passengers at Andheri
articles.summary: MUMBAI: In yet another incident of knifing on a local train in Mumbai, an innocent bystander suffered injuries on Sunday.
articles.body: MUMBAI: In yet another incident of knifing on a local train in Mumbai, an innocent bystander suffered injuries on Sunday. Suresh Sharma was standing in the passage of a Churchgate bound local train when a fight broke out between two other passengers.At Andheri, one of the passengers later identified as Shivaji Gaikwad, took out a knife and tried to stab the man he was fighting with. But he missed and ended up slashing Sharma on the chest.Police said Sharma's shirt was soaked with blood but the train had already begun moving by then. He alighted at Bandra station and was rushed to the Bhabha Hospital where he was administered sutures.Meanwhile police teams tracked down Gaikwad and arrested him on charges of assault. Police said Gaikwad is a Nashik native and worked as a daily wager in Mumbai.After a young passenger, Mayank Lohar, was brutally knifed to death inside a local train compartment earlier this year, police had intensified checks and had warned commuters to not carry sharp weapons or work tools. articles.title: Welsh government pledges to end A&E corridor care by 2029
articles.summary: The Welsh government has vowed to speed up emergency care and help patients get home sooner.
articles.body:
A patient spent more than two days waiting in A&E on two separate occasions - and has vowed never to go back.

Andrew Railton, 63, from Rhondda Cynon Taf, said he sat "on the same chair" at Royal Glamorgan Hospital, in Talbot Green, for more than 50 hours on each visit after suffering from pneumonia, and then "deathly low" potassium levels.

It comes as a £23m plan by the Welsh government promises to end A&E corridor care in Wales by 2029.

Senior emergency doctors have warned too many patients in Wales are experiencing "a terrible time" due to emergency care pressures and delays.

Cwm Taf Morgannwg health board said it was sorry for Railton's experience and the distress caused.

Railton said he was "pretty poorly" and sat in the waiting room for around nine hours before seeing a doctor.

"I was put in the chair and obviously put on the drip... but basically sat in this draughty corridor," he said.

"They brought stools and chairs, and there were people basically just stood around all over the place with drips in them, and it was something Victorian. I was there for 50-odd hours."

A bed was eventually found for him and he stayed in hospital for a further three days.

But a few months later he was told to go back to A&E because of "deathly low" potassium levels.

"Believe it or not, I was put in exactly the same chair that I was in last time. And I sat in that chair overnight while I had a drip administered to me," he said.

Railton says there is "no chance in hell" of him going back to the A&E even if his "leg falls off".

The Welsh government's new emergency care plan points to delays and problems in 2025-26:

Ambulances took an average of two hours and 24 minutes from arrival in hospital to transferring their patients, resulting in 184,850 "lost hours"

Patients aged 85 or over spent an average of seven hours and 13 minutes in A&E with 15% of all cases waiting more than 12 hours

62,346 people admitted as an emergency stayed more than 21 days in hospital

There are around 1,400 patients, at any given time, occupying beds that are clinically ready to leave

With each bed occupied costing £500-£600 a day, the bill to the NHS was £172m

The new plan sets goals for the "whole journey" of the patient - from the scene of the emergency, through to recovery at home.

One of the key milestones is that A&E corridor care or care in other unsuitable spaces should be eliminated by 2029.

Mabon ap Gwynfor, Cabinet Minister for Health and Care, said: "When someone needs emergency care, they should know help will come quickly, they will receive the right care, and they will spend only as long in hospital as they need to.

"Too many people do not experience this consistently today and that must change."

Emergency doctors have frequently warned that patients too often face harm because they are being treated in unsafe spaces in A&E.

Speaking to Politics Wales, Dr Katja Empson, of the Royal College of Emergency Medicine, warned that too many patients were experiencing "terrible" conditions.

"They're often spending a very long time waiting for a bed, and often in a very inappropriate area," she said.

"We are causing harm because people are delayed in the emergency department."

The plan sets out an "ambition" to discharge patients from hospital, where possible, within 72 hours.

It includes making sure patients get early assessments from a senior clinicians, receive quick diagnostic tests and get rapid support from pharmacy and therapy and rehabilitation teams.

Planning for a safe transfer home should happen from the moment a patient arrives, the plan says.

The plan also aims to address relatively poor survival rates for people having cardiac arrests in communities.

It notes that of the 2,800 out-of-hospital cardiac arrests that occur each year - just one in 20 in Wales (5%) survive compared to 8% in England and 10% in Scotland.

There is an ambition for Wales to become a "nation of life-savers" by 2029 by training people to be more confident in cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and raising awareness among children and young people.

New technology will be explored such as drones carrying defibrillators that can save lives.

The "nation of life-savers" aim is supported by Ed Grant, a Welsh Ambulance community first responder who was himself saved by CPR.

The 73-year-old from Barry spent 50 years volunteering in various emergency services.

"I'm actually living proof that CPR works," he said, recalling how his wife kept him alive after he suffered a cardiac arrest at home three years ago.

"Luckily my wife knows CPR because I taught her... she started CPR on me, called the ambulance and called one of my responders as well."

He said community responders can often reach patients first, particularly in rural areas.

"We work very much in tandem with the ambulance service... we can get there first and start dealing with it, keep the person alive and well until the ambulance can arrive," he said.

The plan will include new set of measures and targets which will be recorded and reported on annually from spring next year, with a review in 2030.

These will include measures of patient survival and recovery as well as people's experience of care including corridor care.

Dr Siobhan Lewis, National Clinical Lead for Frailty in NHS Wales and consultant geriatrician, said: "We are already seeing the effects of an ageing population and those living with multiple medical conditions in our acute care areas, and the need for person-centred care has never been greater."

articles.title: Pancreatic cancer mystery deepens as researchers make unexpected discovery
articles.summary: University of Cincinnati study found Black patients' pancreatic tumors had more B cells and cells tied to drug resistance, pointing to tailored care.
articles.body: A University of Cincinnati study found differences in pancreatic tumors that could help explain why that type of cancer affects some patients differently, potentially leading to more personalized treatments. Researchers examined 22 pancreatic tumors from patients of different racial backgrounds across the U.S., looking for differences in cancer cells and how the immune system responds to them. The study included seven Black patients and 15 non-African American patients. The findings were published in the journal Cancer Research. FDA APPROVES ONCE-DAILY PILL FOR DEADLY CANCER AFTER PATIENTS' SURVIVAL RATES NEARLY DOUBLE Tumors from Black patients had fewer of the most common type of pancreatic cancer cells and more cells with a mix of different characteristics, the researchers found. Some of those cell characteristics have been associated with drug resistance, but the study did not establish whether they affected patients’ treatment outcomes. Additionally, tumors from Black patients contained more B cells, a type of immune cell, and larger clusters of immune cells. Researchers found signs that some B cells may suppress the body’s response to cancer, although the significance of these differences is unclear. PATIENTS REMAIN CANCER-FREE NEARLY 3 YEARS AFTER RECEIVING EXPERIMENTAL IMMUNOTHERAPY Dr. Raymond Wadlow, a gastrointestinal medical oncologist at Inova Schar Cancer Institute in Virginia, said that using immunotherapy to help the immune system attack the disease has been particularly challenging in pancreatic cancer. "That's been very difficult to do in pancreatic cancer because the pancreatic tumor subverts the immune system so that it is fighting for it instead of for the host or the rest of the body," Wadlow, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital. The study found no significant differences between groups in the major genetic changes known to drive the disease. Pancreatic cancer is approximately 20% more likely to develop in Black Americans than in non-African Americans, according to the researchers. WHERE YOU LIVE COULD SHAPE YOUR RISK OF CANCER MORTALITY, STUDY SUGGESTS The findings highlight the importance of including patients from different backgrounds in cancer research, according to lead study author Nina Steele, Ph.D., an assistant professor in UC’s College of Medicine. "This study shows that ignoring diverse ancestry in medical research leaves blind spots in the search for a cure," she told Fox News Digital. Wadlow noted that pancreatic cancers can share major DNA mutations but can differ considerably in how their cells behave and interact with nearby immune cells and surrounding tissue. "Those differences may also vary across patient populations, such as between Black and non-Black patients," he told Fox News Digital. "While intriguing, these findings are still a long way from changing patient care." "That is potentially important both for understanding disparities in pancreatic cancer and, ultimately, for developing more individualized treatments." Pancreatic cancer can vary from one tumor to another, and even within the same tumor, Wadlow explained. "The cancer cell itself is only part of the story," he said. The surrounding immune cells and tissue may affect how a tumor behaves and responds to treatment, helping to explain why a single treatment approach may not work for every patient. The findings have several limitations. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Researchers have not established how the intermediate tumor cells affect survival or whether they respond differently to standard chemotherapy, Steele said. The team also needs to study pancreatic tissue from people without cancer to better understand when these differences develop. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Wadlow cautioned that race and genetic ancestry do not fully account for the environmental, socioeconomic and biological factors that could explain the findings. Larger studies involving patients from diverse backgrounds are needed to determine whether these differences affect treatment outcomes or survival, the oncologist said. "While intriguing, these findings are still a long way from changing patient care," he added. Wadlow encouraged newly diagnosed patients to ask about hereditary genetic testing, which can identify inherited mutations that may also affect relatives. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "If we find an inherited mutation, then family members can be tested," he said. Steele said the findings also underscore the need for clinical trials that represent the patients affected by pancreatic cancer. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It is also a reminder for the medical system to ensure that clinical trials reflect the entire population at risk, in order to find treatments that can help all patients, not just some patients," she told Fox News Digital. The research was funded in part by the National Cancer Institute.

articles.title: Haven’t Exercised in a While? This Is the Best Time of Day to Go for a Walk
articles.summary: In TODAY.com’s Expert Tip of the Day, an orthopedic surgeon reveals the best time of day to walk if you’re starting from zero in order to maximize the health benefits.
articles.body: If you’re starting a new fitness journey or getting back into exercise after a long break, you’re not alone. Everyone has to begin somewhere, even if it’s just getting up off the couch. And if you’re starting from zero, walking is one of the best ways to move your body and improve your physical fitness, orthopedic surgeon Dr. Vonda Wright tells TODAY.com. Walking is an accessible, low-impact and science-backed way to boost both physical and mental health. If you’re a beginner, you may set out to walk a certain distance or number of steps at first. But the time of day you choose to go on a walk also matters, says Wright. In order to get the most out of your walk, Wright recommends walking at a specific time of day. Fitness Tip of the Day: Go on A Walk After Eating Your Largest Meal of the Day “...Take a walk after your biggest meal,” says Wright. Whether that’s breakfast, lunch or dinner, try to go on your walk within about 30 minutes to an hour of finishing eating. Why It Matters Going on a walk after eating your largest meal of the day has several advantages, especially if you’re switching from a formerly sedentary lifestyle. Approximately 25% of Americans report getting zero physical activity outside of work, according to data from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Walking is a tremendous way to start moving, says Wright, and strategically timing your walk can maximize the benefits. Going on a walk will get the muscles moving, heart rate up and lungs working harder, which improves cardiovascular health. Activating the muscles, especially the large muscle groups in the lower body, also helps pull glucose out of the bloodstream. And after a meal is when blood sugar tends to spike the highest. Research shows that walking for just two to five minutes after a meal can help manage blood sugar and insulin levels, TODAY.com previously reported. Walking after eating can also aid digestion by speeding up gastrointestinal motility, or the transit time of food moving through our digestive system. Finally, a walk can combat feelings of sluggishness after a large meal, which may help boost mood. How To Get Started If you’re truly starting from zero, Wright recommends walking for just five minutes at first. “Then go up to ten minutes, and eventually work your way up to 30 minutes,” Wright recommends. The ultimate goal should be to walk for at least 30 minutes at a moderate-intensity pace, most days of the week. If you want to make your walks more challenging, try increasing the time or distance, speeding up your pace, walking at an incline or wearing a weighted vest, says Wright. TODAY’s Expert Tip of the Day series is all about simple strategies to make life a little easier. Every Monday through Friday, different qualified experts share their best advice on diet, fitness, heart health, mental wellness and more.
